Stealth, Heists, NPC Reactions and Pursuit

Status: Core pillars confirmed \| 22 November 2026

# The two equally excellent outcomes

A flawless, alarm-free infiltration should be profoundly satisfying. If an alarm sounds, the resultant fight or desperate escape should be so physically spectacular and improvisational that the player wants to play it out, even if survival seems impossible. Reloading should not be the reflexive “correct” response. The transition from stealth to battle should be fluid and unscripted.

# Stealth is systemic

Stealth, sneaking, hiding, diversion and low-noise play should work throughout the world, not in isolated stealth mission rooms. Design a discoverable grammar of sight lines, sound, patrol attention, suspicious activity, hiding places, cover, alarms, locked doors, timing, character size, flight paths, disguise or invisibility where powers permit.

The game's acquired powers and character specialties must support both stealth and combat applications where coherent: grab an enemy quietly into darkness versus suplex them through a wall; sneak away with a vehicle versus use it as a battering ram.

# Heists are discovered opportunities

A guarded bank, jewel room, museum or noble treasury has valuables, inhabitants and plausible physical security. Players decide whether to rob it and how; a specific “begin heist mission” flag should not be necessary for basic interaction. Stealing can create pursuit, alter town relationships, unlock new powers, or reveal unintended routes.

Examples: tiny character through vent; invisibility cloak; social disguise; flying route over roof; excavated entrance; loud frontal assault; party-based distractions. These are candidate approaches, not guaranteed assets or maps.

# NPCs can be provoked

The player can start a fight in a bar or royal chamber, insult or strike a seemingly harmless inhabitant, hijack an operating vehicle, steal valuables, destroy property or otherwise disrupt public life. Like LEGO cantina fights, Zelda chicken retaliation, Skyrim town guards and GTA wanted escalation, the world should react as a participant rather than offer inert background NPCs.

Different NPCs respond differently: flee, scold, retaliate, raise an alarm, summon friends, reveal hidden power, intervene, panic, flee the area, or pursue. Inhabitants retain capacity for surprise; some harmless-looking people may be dangerous.

# Resistance escalation

Early provocation produces local reactions. Continued trouble draws patrols, guards, specialized defenders, vehicles, pursuit squads, armored response or elite champions. The aim is not merely increasing enemy count and HP; each response wave should add a new toy, tactic or possibility—equipment to steal, machines to hijack, enemies worth copying powers from, dangerous collisions, dynamic terrain.

No fixed five-star cap is decided. Escalation can be regionally distinct: village crowd, fortified city, forest creatures, fortress military response, Hall of Legends guardians. The precise cap, spawn logic, heat values, response pacing and faction rules are all open.

# Cooling down and escape

After creating chaos players can hide, flee, change routes, use small tunnels or stealth abilities, abandon stolen vehicles, disappear among NPCs or outrun a pursuit. Resistance should search, investigate and eventually cool off according to legible rules. Avoid instant psychic knowledge of the player's location unless fictional powers justify it.

A narrow escape from apparently hopeless pursuit is a top-tier emotional payoff. Need for Speed: Most Wanted / Blacklist is a benchmark for high-pressure pursuit and crashes.

# Consequences that create gameplay

Being caught may provoke additional combat, confiscation, reputation change, temporary exclusion, intensified defenses or an invitation to escape; specific punishment models are open. Overly harsh permanent failure threatens the sense of joyful experimentation. Yet consequences must be legible and real enough for brilliant escapes and social memory to matter.

Cities may repair property after destruction, argue over the party's role, offer rewards after rescues and set alarms quickly after fresh heists. Avoid abstract “moral penalty” popups dominating player feedback.

# Stealth and mayhem as continuums

Player can act quietly for an hour, accidentally trip a bell, fight a hopelessly large force, hijack a mechanical defender, crash it through barricades and sneak away with one HP. Or they can intentionally provoke the strongest response simply to test their abilities. These are not separate game modes.

# Example heist-turned-legend

After saving a town from a dragon, the heroes receive an invisibility cloak. They steal treasured jewels; angry townspeople chase them into a sealed ruined arena; undead gladiators awaken; thieves and townspeople fight together. This is an illustrative “what if,” not a prescribed mission or required sequence.

# Vision test

A player should be able to complete a guarded route without alarm and feel genuinely proud. Another run should accidentally trigger security and result in a spectacular, enjoyable 5–15 minute battle or escape rather than a frustrating forced reset. Provoking everyday NPCs should create surprising but understandable responses. A pursuit should be escapable through a clever route and realistically also capable of overwhelming the party.

PRIMARY CULTURAL ALERT MECHANIC — OWNER-CONFIRMED 22 NOV 2026

This world's alert system isn't merely criminal “heat.” Nearly everyone adores their predictable role in the Hero's Journey. When the heroes do anything seriously contrary to the expected glorious script, the NPCs are utterly horrified, which causes potentially extreme resistance. But when heroes resume normal, visibly role-appropriate behavior, observers become delighted and reassured surprisingly quickly: “Yup! Just as expected!” This creates an important new social-stealth and escape tactic: reestablish the recognizable story rather than merely break line of sight and wait. Appropriate “hero battles villain” behavior may cause little cultural panic, whereas reckless abuse of a sacred object or attack against the wrong type of figure can shock a whole town. How persistent losses and legal grievances interact with immediate calm remains open.

Detailed mechanics: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jQssgW8w1oXo_14lLhbGHVwWTPef7y2TEU_aCD_nMvQ/edit

ROLE-CONSISTENT CONFLICT IS NOT DISTRESS — OWNER CONFIRMED (22 NOV 2026)

The NPC system has THREE basic modes: BUSINESS AS USUAL / CONFUSION-DISTRESS / ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE. Villains are included. A heroic guard resisting a conventional villain and the villain delighting in villainy can BOTH be in BUSINESS AS USUAL while fighting each other. A villain entering a store to buy a potion politely can create MORE narrative dissonance than villainous robbery. This makes the expected ROLE, not ordinary violence or crime, the primary high-level driver. Continued deviations escalate to all-out rage even among noncombatants; apparently correct conduct can swiftly reassure NPCs. Full behavior brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wuGuCu1RhXXhdWuU55ZcJJ8rZAbCx98mZfdqsyrgMv8/edit

CORE COMBAT DISTINCTION — GOOD-GUY COUNTEROFFENSE VERSUS BAD-GUY SIGNALERS (OWNER DIRECTION, 22 NOV 2026)

The game has TWO deliberately different escalation contexts:

(A) Attacking the good guys. When player heroes attack guards, merchants, townspeople, and other expected friendly roles, the violation of heroic expectations creates the existing three-mode response: business as usual, confusion/distress, then absolute blinding rage. Counteroffense scales upward and may ultimately include guards, bystanders, shopkeepers, pets and reinforcements. Returning to expected behavior can pacify witnesses very quickly. The social response can be absurd and emergent; it does not require a signaler.

(B) Fighting bad guys. Ordinary villainous enemies are scattered through levels in thematically appropriate places, plus defended hostile outposts. Combat between recognized hero and villain is BUSINESS AS USUAL for the villains; they may gleefully fight or pursue without suffering narrative dissonance. Their escalating threat is tactical, through identifiable CALL-REINFORCEMENTS SIGNALERS, inspired by the gameplay structure the user cites from Far Cry 5.

HOSTILE OUTPOST SIGNALER RULE (OWNER-CONFIRMED INTENT)

An enemy must DETECT the player, RECOGNIZE that player as a threat, and REACH/ACTIVATE a signaler to successfully call backup. The signaler is a visible, interactable environmental device or fixture. Players may prevent escalation by avoiding detection, eliminating or otherwise interrupting the would-be caller, destroying/disabling the signaler, clearing the enemies so no one can signal again, or leaving the zone.

Successful calls produce waves of reinforcement that can KEEP SCALING INDEFINITELY while conditions allow further signaling; an outpost fight may become an epic endurance battle or force a retreat. No forced reload for detection. The user's intent does not prescribe whether one activated signal runs continuously or each additional wave requires a new deliberate call: select the most readable, fair implementation in prototyping. An especially clear suggested default is repeatable calls by surviving enemies, each with a visible activation window; this gives players opportunities to regain control after the first alarm.

Destroying the signaler stops future calls but does NOT magically remove reinforcements already summoned. Likewise clearing a wave is not necessarily the same as disabling the signaler if another caller can reach it. Escaping the zone should end further local escalation, with the exact pursuit boundary open.

The enemy layout must make this interesting: mixed patrols, detection cones or simple proximity checks, a clear route to the alarm, alternate entrances, reachable sabotage locations, threats defending the signaler, and optional high-value prizes. Signalers should have recognizable silhouettes and animations; warning icon, bell or flare SFX and arrival cues replace lengthy dialogue.

CO-OP AND SOLO

One player can infiltrate toward the signaler while another draws a patrol away; a flyer reaches an elevated alarm, a small character crawls to a hidden disable switch, a grappler intercepts the caller. Solo players must be able to discover physically valid approaches with the shared character party and powers; do not hard-check multiplayer player count.

PRODUCTION

NO NPC AI. Detection is a simple event/raycast/cone/collider; 'threat recognized' is a scripted role/hostility flag; after recognition, an eligible enemy follows a predefined waypoint route or moves toward a marked signaler; on reaching it, a fixed activation animation / countdown triggers a spawn-wave controller. Signalers are destructible/disableable objects. Spawn types and wave intensities derive from simple authored tables with an active-actor cap. 'Endlessly scaling' means no arbitrary maximum number of waves as long as the players allow calls, NOT infinite simultaneous entities or unbounded computing demand. Treat extra reinforcements as exciting combat gameplay, not a stealth failure screen.

Themed enemy camps need not be lore-heavy: a forest bandit camp, occupied castle corridor, factory guard post or cave fort is enough. Most levels can include scattered enemies without outposts. Not every enemy should be allowed to sound an alarm from anywhere.

OPEN: exact recurring-signal protocol, number of outposts/signalers per area, whether signalers can be repaired, threat identification details, per-wave difficulty curve, how zone escape ends pursuit, whether alarms remain destroyed on revisits.

AUTHORITATIVE CORRECTION — WITNESSES AND REPORTS CONTROL ALL REINFORCEMENTS (22 NOV 2026)

OWNER CONFIRMED: In BOTH good-guy and bad-guy encounters, scaling reinforcements ONLY arrive if some character ACTUALLY SIGNALS FOR HELP. The mere fact of an attack, outrage, an unconscious NPC, or an NPC's violent rage does not automatically notify guards or summon distant reinforcements.

GOOD-GUY EXAMPLE: hero attacks isolated shopkeeper. The merchant may enter distress/rage and personally resist, but if the player knocks them unconscious before they signal and nobody witnesses/hears a completed report, the hero can steal all merchandise and leave WITHOUT an outside police response. Another NPC finding the unconscious merchant later can enter mode 2 (confusion/distress), become more likely to call, and cause an investigation ONLY IF the report succeeds. Good-guy NPCs attempt a report only from mode 2 or 3, NEVER mode 1. A raging shopkeeper can fight by themselves with zero shared wanted level.

SHARED GTA/NFS-INSPIRED WANTED/HEAT: distinguish individual NPC emotional modes 1/2/3 from separately reported area alert/pursuit. Repeated successful reporting or reporting by responders can summon increasingly powerful waves. Exact number of tiers, report-to-level mapping and persistence are OPEN. Stop callers, disable signalers, clear outposts or escape. Completed reports aren't retroactively unsent by a local mood reset, even if observers pacify quickly. A reported but unidentified incident should not grant police psychic knowledge of the escaped perpetrator.

VILLAIN OUTPOSTS: earlier detection → threat-recognition → physically reach signaler → completed activation requirement remains. The owner's phrase restricting modes 2/3 is made in the context of GOOD-GUY witnesses. Whether a villain also needs emotional distress to make a tactical reinforcement call is OPEN, since normal hero-villain fighting is business as usual for them. Do not silently assume either answer.

NO NPC AI. Signalers and calls use event flags, waypoint scripts and readable windups; successful reports trigger bounded simultaneous but potentially unbounded repeated reinforcement waves.

Full updated specification: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wbSNfKLfrUsg9YX5qsRhYX9KwiMX8clXRZZBiuuz8PA/edit

OWNER-RESOLVED VILLAIN SIGNALING REQUIREMENT (22 NOV 2026)

Good-guy witnesses may call only in mode 2 (distress) or 3 (rage). BAD GUYS are different: they can call for help whenever they detect and RECOGNIZE a player character as a threat, including while in mode 1 Business As Usual. They are not cognitively distressed by ordinary hero-villain fighting. Like Zelda BOTW/TOTK lookout horns, they can alert allies; like Far Cry 5 outpost alarms, successfully activated devices may summon reinforcement waves. Merely spotting a hero does NOT spawn help; a visible, interruptible signaling action must complete. NPCs have no AI. This supersedes the previously OPEN question about villain mode-gating. Details: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wbSNfKLfrUsg9YX5qsRhYX9KwiMX8clXRZZBiuuz8PA/edit
